newsitem.title: UK: Fighting in Zaire pushes up cobalt price.
newsitem.headline: Fighting in Zaire pushes up cobalt price.

text.p: Cobalt prices continued to rise on Tuesday due to fighting in Zaire's mineral-rich Shaba province.

Traders said prices were also affected by uncertainty over how long disruption to supplies may last, but added that in the long-term a rebel victory may mean higher production of the metal and lower prices.
Cobalt was in demand after news on Monday that the metals producer Gecamines closed its headquarters in Zaire's second city, Lubumbashi, as rebels advanced.
Following the closure, most market operators questioned by Reuters reckoned at least one month of total supply disruption would be factored into the metal's price.

But they added that anyone who secured effective control of mineral-rich Shaba region would not want to curtail production of a hard currency earner like cobalt for long. And as rebel leader Laurent Kabila was reported to be within a hair's breadth of the mines several market operators are starting to look at long term trading strategies.
"At the moment is would be very silly not to be on the bullish side of the market but that could all change," one trader commented.
The trader said conditions throughout Zaire had potential to become calmer and more organised if Kabila ousted ailing President Mobutu.
Under Mobutu the cobalt and copper mines have lacked investment, analysts say.
"There is huge potential for increased production if hard currency is injected into the mines," a source close to the cobalt market said.
"Kabila could be the person who takes the bull by the horns and encourages foreign investment to flow in," added a trader.

Zaire has recently been producing around 5,000 tonnes of cobalt and 40,000 tonnes of copper a year. The copper is marginal to world supply but the cobalt forms roughly one fifth of global supply of all grades of that metal.
Traders were quick to point out that rebel-held diamond fields were already collecting revenue from sales worth well over $500 million a year.
The rebels have promised to clean up what they allege is a corrupt diamond sector. "They would more than likely promise the same in the cobalt and copper belts," a trader said.
In the early 1980s Zaire produced around 15,000 tonnes of cobalt and 500,000 tonnes of copper. Several traders suggested that these levels could be reached again if investment flows in.

World stocks have been declining but new production and extra volume from upgraded mines could see supply and demand in balance by the year 2000. High grade cobalt, used in aerospace and battery industries, was around $25 per lb (about 500 grams) on Tuesday compared with $19 earlier this year.
